title: An Indian American Congressman Was Detained at Gunpoint in the West Bank. He Says It Made Him More Likely to Run for President.
excerpt: Ro Khanna says armed Israeli settlers surrounded his van with M4 rifles, held his group for over an hour, and the IDF sided with the settlers — an experience he says strengthened his resolve to seek the White House in 2028.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Congressman Ro Khanna was detained by armed Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
  • Khanna's experience has strengthened his resolve to consider a presidential run in 2028.
  • Support for Israel among Democrats has plummeted from 59% in 2018 to 22% in 2023.
  • Khanna's visit highlights shifting political dynamics within the Indian American community.
  • The incident raises questions about U.S. military aid to Israel amid rising tensions.
The settlers came with American-made guns. https://x.com/rashtrapatibhvn/status/2075935889210097758 On Wednesday, a van carrying U.S. Congressman Ro Khanna and his team was surrounded and detained by Israeli settlers wielding M4 rifles while visiting a destroyed Palestinian village in the southern West Bank. The group was held for more than an hour near Khirbet Zanuta, a small hamlet whose residents were forcibly displaced by settler raids following the 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel. "We were at a village that Israeli settlers had destroyed, they had destroyed the school, they had destroyed that village, and we were just looking at it," Khanna told Reuters from the Palestinian village of Turmus Ayya on Thursday. "And these hoodlums come in with machine guns — M4, an American-made machine gun — and they detain us. They block off the road." What happened next cut even deeper for the California Democrat: "They call the IDF and the IDF is on their side, not on the side of the Americans." ## An Indian American Voice in a Shifting Democratic Landscape > **""I'm strongly considering it and I'm more resolved to consider it after this trip," he said."** Khanna, 50, is the son of Indian immigrants and represents California's 17th congressional district in Silicon Valley. Born in Philadelphia to parents who emigrated from Punjab, he has long cited Mahatma Gandhi's legacy as formative to his political identity — a connection that makes his confrontation in a land torn by occupation and displacement especially resonant for Indian Americans watching from thousands of miles away. His aide Cameron Kasky confirmed the group was held for over an hour. They appealed to the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem for help before officers — who appeared to be police — eventually intervened and secured their release. The Israeli military confirmed troops and police were dispatched after receiving a report of settlers blocking vehicles near Khirbet Zanuta and said they "dispersed the Israeli civilians and allowed the vehicles to continue on their way." Neither Israel's police nor the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem responded to requests for comment. ## 'More Resolved' to Run Asked whether he was running for president in 2028, Khanna did not deflect. "I'm strongly considering it and I'm more resolved to consider it after this trip," he said. He is the second Democrat mulling a White House bid to visit the region this week. On Wednesday, Rahm Emanuel, who served as chief of staff to President Barack Obama, said from Tel Aviv that Israeli policies toward Palestinians were eroding support for the U.S.-Israeli alliance. The politics are shifting under the party's feet. Israel's favourability rating among Democrats has collapsed from 59 per cent in 2018 to just 22 per cent in May, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. An increasing number of Democrats in Congress are pressing to cut the $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel — funding that includes the very M4 rifles the settlers used to detain an American congressman.

Khanna's Political Context
›Khanna is a prominent Indian American politician.
›He represents California's 17th district.
›His visit was exclusively Palestinian-led.
›He criticized party leadership's stance on Palestine.
Khanna chose to do an exclusively Palestinian-led visit to the West Bank, forgoing the usual Israeli government briefings that typically accompany congressional delegations. Standing on a hill in Turmus Ayya — a village home to thousands of Palestinian American dual nationals — overlooking a valley dotted with settler outposts, he accused his party's leadership of being "clueless about how much of a moral test Palestine, Gaza and Israel have become." ## What This Means for Indian Americans For the roughly five million Indian Americans in the United States, Khanna's trajectory carries particular weight. He is among the most prominent Indian American voices in national politics — alongside Vice President Kamala Harris's successor figures and other lawmakers such as Raja Krishnamoorthi, Ami Bera, and Pramila Jayapal — and the prospect of an Indian American presidential candidate sharpens the community's stake in his political choices. His stance on Palestinian rights also intersects with a broader reckoning within Indian American political identity. While Hindu American groups have historically aligned with pro-Israel positions, a younger generation of South Asian Americans has increasingly connected Palestinian solidarity with anti-colonial movements across the Global South, including India's own history. "If you're unwilling to speak up for Palestinian human rights, if you're unwilling to speak up against the genocide in Gaza, the apartheid in the West Bank, then you are morally compromised," Khanna said. Israel rejects allegations of genocide in Gaza and denies instituting an apartheid regime in the West Bank, which has a population of about three million Palestinians and around 500,000 Jewish settlers. Most countries and the United Nations regard Israeli settlements in the West Bank as illegal under international law. The midterm elections in November will test whether Khanna's moral framing resonates or repels. For Indian American voters navigating the crosscurrents of identity, geopolitics, and representation, his detention at the hands of settlers armed with American weapons is more than a headline — it is a question about what kind of power they want their community to wield.
